fuller.text: This is an experiment in rats about rearing: standing up on the hind legs to look and sniff around. It asks whether the hippocampus, a brain area needed for remembering places, must be active during rearing for rats to form spatial memories.

sentences.text: This is an experiment in rats about rearing: standing up on the hind legs to look and sniff around.
It asks whether the hippocampus, a brain area needed for remembering places, must be active during rearing for rats to form spatial memories.

fuller.text: Most studies of how the hippocampus supports spatial memory look at times when rats walk around or rest quietly. Rearing gets little attention, though rats do it often and it comes with a strong brain rhythm called theta, which is tied to memory. So whether rearing matters for spatial memory was unknown.

sentences.text: Most studies of how the hippocampus supports spatial memory look at times when rats walk around or rest quietly.
Rearing gets little attention, though rats do it often and it comes with a strong brain rhythm called theta, which is tied to memory.
So whether rearing matters for spatial memory was unknown.

fuller.text: Rats learned a task on a maze with eight arms. First four arms opened with food; after a 4-minute break, all eight opened, with food only in the new four. During the first phase only, a ceiling 3D camera spotted rearing and switched on a laser that silenced the hippocampus through a light-driven protein called halorhodopsin. Each rat had three conditions: no light ('Off'), light during rears ('Rear'), and the same light delayed by 6 seconds ('Delay'). A control group carried only a glowing marker protein, with no halorhodopsin.

During the first phase only, a ceiling 3D camera spotted rearing and switched on a laser that silenced the hippocampus through a light-driven protein called halorhodopsin.
Each rat had three conditions: no light ('Off'), light during rears ('Rear'), and the same light delayed by 6 seconds ('Delay').
A control group carried only a glowing marker protein, with no halorhodopsin.

fuller.text: The main results, from 6 experimental and 7 control rats, were these. Silencing during rears cut the share of correct first four choices from 77.7% to 65.7%. It also raised the arms entered to find all food from 5.1 to 6.5. Delayed silencing gave no significant drop in correct choices (72.0%) and only a borderline rise in arms entered (5.9). Light had no significant effect in the control group in any condition.

fuller.text: The authors note the 6-second delay still overlapped about 35.5% of rearing time, so it did not fully separate light from rearing. Nearly every rear leaned a paw on a wall, so the study cannot compare leaning and free-standing rears. It also cannot say whether every rear counts, or whether the same memory forming could happen without rearing.

fuller.text: The conclusion is that activity in the upper (dorsal) hippocampus during rearing is important for spatial memory. The authors suggest silencing may have stopped rats updating their mental map of the room with what they saw while rearing.

brief.text: Rats often stand up on their hind legs to look around, which scientists call rearing. This study asked whether the hippocampus, a brain area key for remembering places, matters during those moments. Its role while rats walk or rest is well studied, but its role during rearing was unknown.

brief.text: In an experiment with rats, scientists switched off this brain area with light, only while rats reared. Later, the rats remembered a maze worse, scoring about 66% instead of 78%. The authors conclude that brain activity during rearing helps rats build memories of places.
